metadata.note:
Passenger rail at Columbus, Indiana, 1844-2003 - added 2026-08-27 to fill a hole in this dataset that reached about 30 mi in every direction: nothing in data/ came within 30 mi of the city. Four corridors are covered. (1) The Madison & Indianapolis, Indiana's first railroad, whose track reached Columbus in July 1844 and ran through to Indianapolis on 1 October 1847; the rival Jeffersonville Railroad arrived from the south in August 1852, the two combined as the JM&I in 1866, and the through Indianapolis-Louisville route became a Pennsylvania Railroad line in 1890, then Penn Central, then Amtrak's Floridian to 1974 and the Kentucky Cardinal from 1999 to 2003. (2) The original Madison line, demoted to a branch in 1866, whose passengers lasted until a mixed-train coach came off on 10 October 1938. (3) The Columbus, Hope & Greensburg of 1884, worked by the CIStL&C and then the Big Four, which lost its last passenger coach on 13 December 1941. (4) The Indianapolis-Columbus-Seymour interurban, electric cars from 19 September 1902 under three successive owners, killed by a head-on collision south of Columbus on 8 September 1941.

Two of the four have honest geometry problems, both stated on the features themselves: the Columbus-Hope end of the Columbus, Hope & Greensburg is a straight-line chord, and the interurban is not drawn on its own right of way at all but on the parallel Pennsylvania Railroad alignment. Read each feature's geometry_quality before taking a distance off this file.
metadata.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap, fetched 2026-08-27. Route relations 9344163 (LIRC Louisville Secondary) and 2234827 (CSX Indianapolis Terminal Subdivision Louisville Secondary Branch) pulled whole from the OSM API and chained by shared node ids; plus Overpass bbox dumps of abandoned and disused railway ways around Columbus, filtered on old_railway_operator=PRR for the Madison branch and old_railway_operator=NYC for the Columbus, Hope & Greensburg. Douglas-Peucker simplified at 25 m.
metadata.mileage_check: Indianapolis-Louisville 107.1 mi against a documented ~110, with Columbus at 40.9 mi from Indianapolis against ~41. Madison branch 44.6 mi against ~45. Columbus-Greensburg 26.8 mi against ~25, but a third of it is chord rather than trace.
not_yet_sourced: Neither Amtrak feature is known to have stopped at Columbus. The Floridian and Kentucky Cardinal features draw passenger trains running ON the line through Columbus; whether either called there has not been established, and the Kentucky Cardinal article names only Jeffersonville south of Indianapolis.

The last year a scheduled train actually stopped at Columbus in the Pennsylvania Railroad and Penn Central era is not sourced. Those features are drawn for the years the corridor carried passenger trains, which is not the same claim.

The interurban's real alignment is not drawn - see the geometry_quality on those four features. Someone with a Baist or USGS-era map of Bartholomew County could replace the borrowed steam-road geometry with the traction company's own.
The Columbus-Hope third of the Columbus, Hope & Greensburg is a 13.38 km straight chord. OSM has no trace of it.

Every headway_min in this file is an estimate. The only frequency figure with a source behind it is the Indiana Railroad's thirty-six daily runs after 1939, and turning that into a headway was my arithmetic, not the source's.
The interurban's opening dates at Greenwood, Franklin, Columbus and Seymour are taken from a search summary of the Indiana Historical Society collection guide rather than read off the guide itself.

Interstate Public Service and Indiana Railroad through service to Louisville, south of Seymour via Scottsburg and Sellersburg, is not drawn; nor is the Indianapolis-Greensburg interurban by way of Shelbyville.
The Columbus, Hope & Greensburg's own passenger service before 1928 has no frequency source; the one-train-a-day figure is documented only from 27 February 1928.
sources: https://indyencyclopedia.org/madison-and-indianapolis-railroad/ (Madison & Indianapolis: state project from 1836, private company February 1843, track at Columbus July 1844, Edinburgh September 1845, first Madison-Indianapolis train 1 October 1847, 1866 Jeffersonville takeover)

https://abandonedonline.net/location/madison-indianapolis-railroad/ (Madison branch: dedicated passenger service ended 15 August 1935, coach on the daily local freight until 10 October 1938; 1890 PCC&StL; 16.8 mi North Vernon-Rossman dismantled 1975; Madison incline 7,012 ft at 5.89 per cent, Reuben Wells from 1868)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Public_Service (Interstate Public Service incorporated 5 September 1912; acquired the Indianapolis, Columbus and Southern Traction, itself formed 20 November 1902; Indianapolis-Louisville route paralleling the Pennsylvania Railroad; Indiana Railroad 1931; south of Seymour abandoned 31 October 1939; 8 September 1941 collision south of Columbus ended service)

metadata.rule_notes: Rule 1: every feature stops at the end of its passenger service - the Madison branch at 1938 though the Madison Railroad still works the south end for freight, the Columbus, Hope & Greensburg at 1941 though it was not abandoned until 1973, the main line at 2003 though the Louisville & Indiana runs it today. Rule 7: the four traction features are mode 'interurban' and draw dashed - the line was built to join separate towns, and its own account describes it running town to town beside the steam road. Rule 4: Pennsylvania Railroad (#7B241C), Penn Central (#1A1A1A), the Big Four (#5C677D) and Amtrak (#1c4e80) reuse this dataset's existing colors; the Madison & Indianapolis (#827717), the Cincinnati, Indianapolis, St. Louis & Chicago (#33691E), the Indianapolis, Columbus & Southern Traction (#AD1457), Interstate Public Service (#00838F) and the Indiana Railroad (#311B92) are new to it. The Jeffersonville Railroad and the JM&I share one color (#3E2723) deliberately: the JM&I is the Jeffersonville company continuing under a new name after absorbing the Madison & Indianapolis, not a separate operator.

Until 1 August 1974 it ran Chicago-Florida by way of Indianapolis and Louisville, which put it over this line through Columbus; deteriorating Penn Central track then pushed it onto the L&N via Evansville, bypassing both cities. properties.company: Cincinnati, Indianapolis, St. Louis and Chicago Railway
properties.line: Cincinnati, Indianapolis, St. Louis & Chicago: Columbus – Greensburg
properties.speed_source: estimated: a rural branch worked by one train a day each way; estimated; no timetable consulted
properties.geometry_quality: PARTLY APPROXIMATE - 26.8 mi drawn against a Columbus-Greensburg route of roughly 25 mi. Only the Hope-Burney-Greensburg portion is real: 15.2 mi chained from railway=abandoned ways tagged old_railway_operator=NYC. The Columbus-Hope end is A 13.38 km STRAIGHT-LINE CHORD - OSM holds no trace of it, and the local rail-trail candidates in Columbus turned out to be the city's People Trail greenway, not this right of way. A further 2.38 km bridge carries the east end onto the ex-Big Four main line, which is then followed the last stretch into Greensburg. Read the western third as a corridor, not a survey.

segments.note: The Columbus, Hope & Greensburg was the surviving fragment of an 1878 scheme for a Cincinnati-St. Louis narrow gauge across Indiana. Chartered first as the Hope & Greensburg and renamed in 1881, it opened to Hope on 2 October 1883 - marked by carrying 152 passengers from Hope to Cincinnati - and to Columbus on 1 April 1884. From May 1884 the Cincinnati, Indianapolis, St. Louis & Chicago worked it, which is why the operating company rather than the owning one carries the color here. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 1878 origins, the 1881 renaming, the 2 October 1883 opening to Hope, the 1 April 1884 opening to Columbus and the CIStL&C operating agreement from May 1884, all from Indiana Transportation History. Headway unsourced.

segments.note: Leased by the Cleveland, Cincinnati, Chicago & St. Louis - the Big Four - on 17 October 1891. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 17 October 1891 Big Four lease from Indiana Transportation History; headway unsourced.

segments.note: By the late 1920s the branch was losing its traffic: passengers had already moved to a bus the railway itself ran, and in 1928 the mail went to a star route bus. From 27 February 1928 the Big Four ran a combined passenger and freight train over the whole line, one train daily - to Columbus in the morning, to Greensburg in the afternoon. The last passenger car, a single coach in a freight consist, came off on 13 December 1941, by which time passenger receipts were reported as low as $2 a month. The line itself was abandoned by Penn Central by 1973 but nothing is drawn past 1941.
sources: Segment-level: the 1928 loss of the mail, the 27 February 1928 combined train with its one-train-a-day pattern, the 13 December 1941 removal of the last passenger car and the $2-a-month receipts, all from Indiana Transportation History quoting the Rushville Republican of 17 December 1941.

properties.company: Indianapolis, Columbus and Southern Traction Company
properties.line: Indianapolis, Columbus & Southern Traction: Indianapolis – Columbus
properties.speed_source: estimated: interurban running on private right of way between towns and street track within them; estimated; no timetable consulted
properties.geometry_quality: NOT THE INTERURBAN'S OWN RIGHT OF WAY. OSM holds no usable trace of the Indianapolis-Columbus-Seymour traction line - a wide sweep for abandoned, disused and razed railway ways between Indianapolis and Seymour returned only unrelated steam-road grades and a few sub-mile fragments near Franklin. This feature is therefore drawn on the parallel Pennsylvania Railroad alignment (the LIRC trace described on the steam-road features), which Wikipedia's account of Interstate Public Service describes the interurban as running alongside, and which served the same towns in the same order: Greenwood, Franklin, Edinburgh, Columbus, Seymour. The real line ran within roughly a mile of this for most of the way but is not this line. Distances taken from it are the steam road's, not the traction company's.

segments.note: Electric cars reached Columbus from Indianapolis on 19 September 1902, working south from Greenwood (1900) and Franklin (6 June 1901). The company took the Indianapolis, Columbus and Southern Traction name on 20 November 1902. Tagged interurban under Rule 7 - it was built to link separate towns, not to serve one built-up area - so it draws dashed. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 20 November 1902 incorporation of the IC&S out of the 1894 Indianapolis, Greenwood and Franklin from the Wikipedia article on Interstate Public Service; the 19 September 1902 arrival at Columbus and the Greenwood and Franklin dates from the Indiana Historical Society's interurban collection guide. Headway unsourced.

segments.note: Amalgamated in 1931 with the other statewide interurbans into the Indiana Railroad. The line south of Seymour was abandoned on 31 October 1939, but Indianapolis-Seymour service carried on, still at thirty-six runs a day. Headway estimated from those thirty-six daily runs read as eighteen each way.
sources: Segment-level: the 1931 amalgamation into the Indiana Railroad and the 31 October 1939 abandonment south of Seymour from the Wikipedia article; the thirty-six daily runs from the same account. The conversion of that figure into a headway is mine, not sourced.

segments.note: Cut back to a single daily round trip in the last stretch - the sources say only 'by 1941', so the 1940 split year is approximate. On the morning of 8 September 1941 a passenger car hit a work train south of Columbus, destroying half the remaining rolling stock; service stopped and was never restarted. This was one of the last interurbans in Indiana.
sources: Segment-level: the reduction to one daily round trip 'by 1941' and the 8 September 1941 collision south of Columbus after which service ceased, from the Wikipedia article. The 1940 boundary is an approximation of 'by 1941', not a sourced date.
